title: Find the department that has the highest average salary.
shortTitle: Find the department that has the highest average salary

s1_definition.profdef: You compute average salary per department with `groupingBy(dept, averagingDouble(salary))`, then take the entry with the maximum average via `max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())`, returning the department name as an `Optional`.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya works out the average pay in each department, then picks the department with the biggest average.
s1_definition.oneliner: Average by department, then `max(comparingByValue())` for the top-average department.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You compute average salary per department with `groupingBy(dept, averagingDouble(salary))`, then take the entry with the maximum average via `max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())`, returning the department name as an `Optional`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya works out the average pay in each department, then picks the department with the biggest average.

**One line to remember:** Average by department, then `max(comparingByValue())` for the top-average department.

sections.s2_technical:
First build `Map<String, Double>` with `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, averagingDouble(Employee::getSalaryAsDouble))`. Then `map.entrySet().stream().max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())` returns the entry with the greatest average, and reading getKey gives the department. max returns an Optional to cover an empty input.

This is a two-stage computation: aggregate then select the maximum aggregate. It is clearer than trying to do both at once, and each stage is independently testable. The averagingDouble gives a Double average per department which the comparator compares.

The senior nuance is tie-breaking and precision. If two departments share the top average, max returns one arbitrary winner, so I chain thenComparing on the department name for determinism. Averages use double which is fine for ranking; exact reporting would use BigDecimal. I guard null departments. The pattern of "aggregate then argmax over the aggregates" is extremely common in analytics.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A compensation review at the National Bank of India must identify the department with the highest average salary.

This is exactly what average-by-department then max-by-value does — it finds the top-average department.

The code defines a `CompReviewService.deptWithHighestAvg method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT 1,000,000, Amit IT 600,000, Priya Sales 900,000.

Step 1: averagingDouble gives IT an average of 800,000 and Sales an average of 900,000.

Step 2: max by value compares 800,000 and 900,000.

Step 3: Sales wins with the higher average.

Step 4: Reading the key returns Sales.

```
INFO: Highest avg salary dept: Sales
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find the department with the highest average salary I use a two-stage computation. First I group by department and average the salaries with averagingDouble, giving a map from department to its average pay. Then I take the entry with the maximum average using max with comparingByValue and read its key, which is the department. max returns an Optional so an empty input is handled safely.

I keep these two stages separate — aggregate, then select the maximum of the aggregates — because it is clearer and each stage is independently testable, and it is the same argmax-over-aggregates pattern that shows up throughout analytics. At the National Bank of India this backs a compensation review that flags the top-paying department on average.

The senior point I stress is tie-breaking and precision. If two departments share the top average, max returns an arbitrary winner, so I chain thenComparing on the department name to make the result deterministic. The double averages are perfectly fine for ranking, but for an authoritative published figure I would compute the averages in BigDecimal with explicit rounding. I also guard against null departments so a missing value does not create a spurious bucket.
